record.paper_title: High Open-Circuit Voltages in Lead-Halide Perovskite Solar Cells – Experiment, Theory and Open Questions
record.context_brief: Built-in voltage and contact band diagrams
record.original_question: In lead-halide perovskite solar cells, how does the built-in voltage Vbi, set by contact work-function and perovskite band-edge alignment, practically control performance, minority-carrier concentrations at electron and hole contact interfaces, and interfacial recombination; and what actual band diagram, work-function alignment, and contact-layer energy-level structure allow devices using PTAA and PCBM contact materials with ITO and Ag conductive electrodes to suppress interfacial recombination even when the expected work-function difference appears too small?

evidence.quote: Note that the exact dependence of Voc on S also depends on the minority carrier concentration at the two contacts which are determined in turn by the differences between contact workfunction and conduction band (at the cathode) or valence band (at the anode) of the perovskite. Here we use an offset of 0.1 eV on each side which leads to a built-in voltage Vbi = 1.4 eV (band gap minus twice the offset of 0.1 eV).

Finally, an open question is the practical influence of the built-in voltage Vbi on solar cell performance. Charge carrier diffusion lengths are generally reported to be high enough to achieve efficient charge collection via diffusion within absorbers with thicknesses of less than a micron. However, the built-in voltage still affects the concentration of minority carriers at the interfaces to electron and hole contact materials. Only a high Vbi reduces the minority carrier concentration sufficiently to suppress recombination at these interfaces.

However, it is often not clear whether the values of Vbi leading to optimum power conversion efficiency in Fig. 8 are consistent with the expected workfunction difference between the contacts. For instance, for the high Voc device discussed in ref. [35], the electron and hole contact materials (PTAA and PCBM) are fairly intrinsic and the highly conductive materials ITO and Ag should not have a sufficiently high workfunction difference to enable efficient suppression of interfacial recombination. Nevertheless, the cells are in practice able to suppress recombination quite efficiently. This suggests that we lack knowledge on how the band diagram of the cell looks like and how the workfunctions and energy levels of the contact and absorber layers enable such low interfacial recombination rates (even if we do understand the low recombination velocities).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a thin-film lead-halide perovskite solar cell modeled as a one-dimensional heterostructure consisting of: a transparent conductive electrode of indium tin oxide (ITO), a hole-transport contact layer of poly[bis(4-phenyl)(2,4,6-trimethylphenyl)amine] (PTAA), a lead-halide perovskite absorber of band gap E_g ≈ 1.6 eV and thickness less than 1 μm, an electron-transport contact layer of [6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM), and a silver (Ag) back electrode. Define the built-in voltage V_bi of the device as V_bi = E_g − Δ_c − Δ_a, where Δ_c is the energy offset between the cathode contact work function and the perovskite conduction-band minimum and Δ_a is the offset between the anode contact work function and the perovskite valence-band maximum. Assume drift–diffusion transport with bulk minority-carrier diffusion lengths exceeding the absorber thickness, and let S denote the interfacial recombination velocity at the contacts. The minority-carrier concentrations n_min(0) at the hole contact and p_min(L) at the electron contact, and consequently the interfacial recombination current J_rec ≈ q·S·n_min, are controlled by V_bi through the equilibrium band bending. 

(a) Derive, within a standard drift–diffusion model with Boltzmann statistics, an explicit expression for the dependence of the open-circuit voltage V_oc on V_bi and S that exposes how only a sufficiently large V_bi suppresses interfacial recombination by reducing the minority-carrier densities at the two contact interfaces.

(b) Construct an equilibrium band diagram (specifying the work functions of ITO and Ag, the HOMO/LUMO levels and any interfacial dipoles of PTAA and PCBM, and the perovskite band edges) that is quantitatively consistent with the experimentally observed efficient suppression of interfacial recombination in PTAA/perovskite/PCBM devices with ITO and Ag electrodes, despite the nominal work-function difference between ITO and Ag being too small to produce a V_bi close to E_g.

(c) Identify the mechanism (e.g., Fermi-level pinning, interfacial dipoles at PTAA/perovskite or PCBM/Ag interfaces, doping of the contact layers, or band bending inside the contact layers) that allows the effective V_bi seen by minority carriers to approach the value required for low interfacial recombination, and quantify the magnitude of the required dipole or pinning energy.
artifact.status_search_result: The question concerns an explicitly stated open problem in lead-halide perovskite photovoltaics: reconciling the band-diagram and work-function alignment in PTAA/perovskite/PCBM devices with ITO and Ag electrodes with the experimentally observed strong suppression of interfacial recombination. Recent literature (2020–2025) on energy-level alignment, Fermi-level pinning, and interfacial dipoles in such stacks continues to investigate this, but no consensus quantitative band diagram has been established, so the problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Energy-level alignment at interfaces in metal-halide perovskite solar cells
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews persistent uncertainties in band alignment and Fermi-level pinning at perovskite/charge-transport-layer interfaces.
status_evidence.claim: The detailed band diagrams and effective built-in voltages of perovskite/PTAA and perovskite/PCBM contacts remain debated.

status_evidence.title: Interface recombination in perovskite solar cells
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses how built-in potential and interface energetics, rather than bulk diffusion lengths, limit V_oc in modern perovskite cells.
status_evidence.claim: Interfacial recombination control via V_bi continues to be an active and unresolved area.
